Soil respiration is the release of carbon dioxide (CO₂) from soil, mostly by microorganisms that break down organic matter. Students investigated how temperature, moisture, and the supply of organic carbon affect the rate of soil respiration.

In each trial, a 200 g core of soil collected from a single meadow was placed in a sealed 1 L glass jar. After 24 hours, the CO₂ concentration in the air inside the jar was measured with an infrared gas analyzer and converted to a CO₂ flux, in milligrams of CO₂ per kilogram of soil per hour (mg/kg/h).

Study 1
Four cores were adjusted to a moisture content of 25% by mass and incubated at 5 °C, 15 °C, 25 °C, or 35 °C (Trials 1-4, Table 1).

Study 2
Five cores were incubated at 25 °C after being adjusted to a moisture content of 5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, or 45% by mass (Trials 5-9).

Study 3
Four cores were adjusted to 25% moisture and incubated at 25 °C. Before incubation, 1.0 g of glucose dissolved in 5 mL of water was mixed into two of the cores; 5 mL of water alone was mixed into the other two. One core from each pair was first autoclaved (heated under pressure to 121 °C for 30 min) and allowed to cool before anything was mixed in (Trials 10-13).

graphic.caption: Table 1. Conditions and measured CO₂ flux for each trial of Studies 1-3.

prompt: Which of the following factors was varied in Study 1 but held constant in Study 2?
choices: Moisture content of the soil
Incubation temperature
Mass of each soil core
Length of the incubation
explanation: Study 1 incubated cores at four temperatures (5 °C to 35 °C) with moisture fixed at 25%; Study 2 held the temperature at 25 °C and varied moisture, so "Incubation temperature" is the factor varied only in Study 1. Core mass (200 g) and incubation time (24 hours) were the same in every trial.
subskill: identify the independent variable of a study

A capacitor stores electric charge. When a charged capacitor is connected across a resistor, charge flows through the resistor and the voltage across the capacitor decreases over time. Students studied how the rate of this decrease depends on the resistance R, the capacitance C, and the initial voltage V₀.

In each trial, a capacitor was charged to V₀ with a power supply, then disconnected from the supply and connected across a resistor at time t = 0. A data logger recorded the capacitor voltage every 0.1 s. The discharge time, t_d, was defined as the time at which the voltage had fallen to 37% of V₀. Each trial was repeated three times, and the average t_d was recorded.

Study 1
A 470 μF capacitor was charged to V₀ = 9.0 V and discharged through a resistor of 10 kΩ, 22 kΩ, 47 kΩ, or 100 kΩ (Figure 1).

Study 2
A 47 kΩ resistor was used with a 100 μF, 220 μF, 470 μF, or 1,000 μF capacitor, each charged to V₀ = 9.0 V (Figure 1).

Study 3
The 470 μF capacitor was discharged through the 47 kΩ resistor after being charged to V₀ = 3.0 V, 6.0 V, 9.0 V, or 12.0 V. The values of t_d were 22.2 s, 22.0 s, 22.3 s, and 22.1 s, respectively.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Average discharge time t_d for each trial of Study 1 (S1: 470 μF capacitor, resistance varied) and Study 2 (S2: 47 kΩ resistor, capacitance varied).

prompt: According to Figure 1, in Study 1, t_d for the 47 kΩ resistor was approximately how many times as great as t_d for the 10 kΩ resistor?
explanation: Figure 1 gives t_d of about 22.3 s for 47 kΩ and 4.8 s for 10 kΩ; 22.3 ÷ 4.8 is about 4.6, so the closest value is "5."

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. Heating an enzyme can increase the rate of the reaction it catalyzes, but heat can also unfold the protein and permanently destroy its activity. Researchers studied the effect of temperature on an esterase, an enzyme isolated from a soil fungus that converts a colorless ester into a yellow product.

In each trial, 2.0 mL of buffer solution (pH 7.0) containing 0.10 mg of the enzyme was placed in a water bath at a set temperature. From this measurement, the initial reaction rate, in micromoles of product per minute (μmol/min), was calculated.

Study 1
The pre-incubation period was 1 min. Trials were conducted at 20 °C, 30 °C, 40 °C, 50 °C, 60 °C, and 70 °C (Figure 1).

Study 2
The procedure of Study 1 was repeated, except that the pre-incubation period was 30 min (Figure 1).

Study 3
The procedure of Study 2 was repeated, except that the buffer solution also contained 20% glycerol by volume, a compound thought to stabilize protein structure (Figure 1).

passage:
Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. Heating an enzyme can increase the rate of the reaction it catalyzes, but heat can also unfold the protein and permanently destroy its activity. Researchers studied the effect of temperature on an esterase, an enzyme isolated from a soil fungus that converts a colorless ester into a yellow product.

In each trial, 2.0 mL of buffer solution (pH 7.0) containing 0.10 mg of the enzyme was placed in a water bath at a set temperature. After a pre-incubation period at that temperature, 0.10 mL of ester solution was added, and the increase in yellow color over the next 60 s was measured with a spectrophotometer. From this measurement, the initial reaction rate, in micromoles of product per minute (μmol/min), was calculated.

Study 1
The pre-incubation period was 1 min. Trials were conducted at 20 °C, 30 °C, 40 °C, 50 °C, 60 °C, and 70 °C (Figure 1).

Study 2
The procedure of Study 1 was repeated, except that the pre-incubation period was 30 min (Figure 1).

Study 3
The procedure of Study 2 was repeated, except that the buffer solution also contained 20% glycerol by volume, a compound thought to stabilize protein structure (Figure 1).
